content: Endometrial cancer is one of the most prevalent gynecological malignancies in developed nations. For advanced stages of this disease, treatment typically involves radiotherapy, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, or combinations of these modalities. However, survival outcomes for patients with advanced or metastatic endometrial cancer remain poor, highlighting the urgent need for more effective systemic treatment options that can improve both survival and safety outcomes. The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway is frequently dysregulated in endometrial cancer, and single-arm studies have shown promising results with the use of PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors in advanced or recurrent cases. The objective of this research was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatment regimens containing PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors in women with locally advanced, metastatic, or recurrent endometrial cancer. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and Embase up to January 16, 2019. Additional searches were performed in the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov in July 2018. Reference lists from included studies and endometrial cancer guidelines were also reviewed. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared regimens containing PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors, either as monotherapy or in combination with other treatments (e.g., chemotherapy or hormonal therapy), against regimens without these inhibitors. There were no restrictions on the type of comparator regimens. Data were independently extracted, and the risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed. The primary outcomes of interest were progression-free survival (PFS) and grade 3/4 toxicity. Secondary outcomes included overall survival (OS), objective tumor response rate, quality of life, and treatment-related mortality. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence for key outcomes. Two RCTs involving a total of 361 women were included in the analysis. One study investigated the effects of the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus in combination with carboplatin and paclitaxel, compared to carboplatin, paclitaxel, and bevacizumab in treatment-naïve women with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. The second study compared the mTOR inhibitor ridaforolimus as monotherapy against progestin or investigator-selected chemotherapy in women who had previously received treatment for metastatic or recurrent endometrial cancer. Additionally, five ongoing studies were identified, focusing on the effects of PI3K and AKT inhibitors, metformin, and dual mTOR inhibitors. For first-line therapy, the use of an mTOR inhibitor-containing regimen may worsen progression-free survival compared to standard chemotherapy (hazard ratio [HR] 1.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.06 to 1.93; one study, 231 participants; low-certainty evidence). In contrast, for secondor third-line therapy, an mTOR inhibitor-containing regimen likely improves progression-free survival compared to chemotherapy or endocrine therapy (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.91; one study, 95 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Regarding toxicity, data from both studies indicated that mTOR inhibitor regimens may increase the risk of grade 3/4 mucositis (risk ratio [RR] 10.42, 95% CI 1.34 to 80.74; two studies, 357 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, these regimens may result in little to no difference in the risk of anemia or interstitial pneumonitis (low-certainty evidence for both toxicities). Overall, the event rates for these toxicities were low. In terms of overall survival, an mTOR inhibitor-containing regimen may result in little to no difference compared to chemotherapy in first-line therapy (HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.78; one study, 231 participants; low-certainty evidence). A similar finding was observed for secondor third-line therapy (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.61; one study, 130 participants; low-certainty evidence). Tumor response rates also showed little to no difference between mTOR inhibitor regimens and chemotherapy or hormonal therapy in both first-line and second-/third-line settings (first-line: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.17; one study, 231 participants; second-/third-line: RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.40; one study, 61 participants; low-certainty evidence). Neither study reported data on quality of life. In conclusion, the evidence from these two RCTs is of low certainty. In the context of recurrent disease, mTOR inhibitors may improve progression-free survival, but no clear benefit was observed in overall survival or tumor response rates. The results of at least five ongoing studies are awaited to better understand the role of PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors in the treatment of advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. Until these findings are available, definitive conclusions regarding their clinical utility cannot be drawn.
